canonical_topic: Expected-value example: aggressive bidding trade-off by cost basis
definition: The author's numeric illustration comparing a near-zero-cost plant and a high-cost ($95) plant deciding whether to bid aggressively for a $1 price increase, given a 10% chance the aggressive bid leaves the plant undispatched.
core_idea: For a plant with a large profit margin, the expected loss from occasionally not clearing outweighs the expected gain from a small price increase, while for a plant with a thin margin the same trade-off favors bidding aggressively.
key_points: Setup: power price is roughly $100, and bidding aggressively can push the price up by $1 but carries a 10% chance of the plant not being dispatched at all.

Near-zero-cost plant: a 10% chance of losing the full $100 profit (~$10 expected loss) is weighed against an extra $1, 90% of the time (~$0.90 expected gain) — the trade-off does not favor aggressive bidding.

High-cost plant with a $95 cost basis (only $5 profit at $100 price): a 10% chance of losing that $5 profit (~$0.50 expected loss) is weighed against the same ~$0.90 expected gain from the price bump — here aggressive bidding is worthwhile.
The comparison shows the incentive to bid aggressively increases as a plant's built-in profit margin (price minus cost) shrinks.
trading_implications: Expect higher-cost, thinner-margin generators to be more willing to bid aggressively to move price, while very profitable low-cost generators tend to bid passively to protect guaranteed dispatch.
